opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about those numbers is that they're not something to memorize for its own sake. They're the raw material for back-of-the-envelope calculations, which I think is one of the most underrated skills in designing systems.

Before you write a lot of code, you often have several plausible designs. You can get a surprisingly good sense of which one will work by writing down a few rough estimates. How many disk seeks does this need? How much data am I pulling over the network? Can this fit in memory, or am I going to main memory or disk on every request? Am I crossing a datacenter boundary? If you know a main memory reference is on the order of 100 nanoseconds, a disk seek is on the order of 10 milliseconds, and a round trip within a datacenter is around half a millisecond, you can often rule out a design in five minutes. Otherwise you might spend weeks building it before finding out it's off by a factor of a hundred.

The thing that matters is the ratios between these numbers, more than the absolute values. Hardware has changed a lot since that list was first put together. Flash changed the storage picture a lot, networks got faster, and now we care about things like accelerator memory bandwidth and interconnect between chips. But the relative relationships still teach you the right instincts. Sequential access is much cheaper than random access. Locality really matters. Batching amortizes fixed costs. Going across the network or to disk is expensive enough that it should be a deliberate choice.

So my advice is to internalize the orders of magnitude and keep your own updated version for the hardware you actually use. Then make a habit of doing that quick arithmetic early. Will this image-thumbnail page take 30 milliseconds or three seconds? Do I need ten machines or a thousand? Those calculations won't be exact, but being within a factor of two or so is usually enough to make a good decision. Then, of course, you build a prototype and measure, because the real system will always surprise you somewhere.

r001.rationale: The response says latency figures are raw material for back-of-the-envelope calculations and uses them to compare plausible designs before implementation.

r002.rationale: It recommends internalizing latency orders of magnitude for hardware operations, but does not address building execution-time intuitions for operations in the higher-level libraries a programmer uses.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that the exact numbers don't matter nearly as much as the relationships between them. If you remember that an L1 cache reference is about half a nanosecond, main memory is around a hundred nanoseconds, a round trip within a datacenter is a few hundred microseconds, and reading a megabyte sequentially off disk is on the order of a few milliseconds, then you have a mental model that spans roughly seven or eight orders of magnitude. That's the useful part. You don't need to know whether it's 100 nanoseconds or 120, you need to know that going to memory is two hundred times more expensive than hitting cache, and that going across the network is a thousand times more expensive than that.

The way I use them, and the way I'd encourage people to use them, is for back-of-the-envelope calculations before you write any code. Say you're designing a system that has to serve a request in under 100 milliseconds. You can sit down and say: okay, I'm going to touch this many machines, each of those is a network round trip, I'm going to read this much data off disk or from memory, I need to do this many random lookups. You add it all up and in about ten minutes you know whether the design is feasible at all, or whether you're off by a factor of a hundred and need to rethink things. It's remarkable how often people skip that step and discover the problem only after building the whole thing.

The other thing those numbers teach you is where to spend your effort. If a sequential read of a megabyte from memory is a quarter of a millisecond, but a single disk seek is ten milliseconds, then you should go to great lengths to make your data layout sequential and avoid seeks. If you're doing something that requires lots of small random accesses, you want it in memory, or you want to batch the requests. Compression starts to look very attractive when you realize that the CPU cost of decompressing a block is tiny compared to pulling that block over the network or off a disk. A lot of the design decisions in systems like Bigtable or Spanner fall directly out of that kind of reasoning.

I'd also say the numbers encourage you to think about parallelism and fan-out correctly. One round trip in a datacenter might be half a millisecond, but if you're waiting on a hundred of them, the tail matters a lot, because you're bound by the slowest one. So you start thinking about hedged requests, or sending backup requests after a short delay, or doing the work in fewer round trips. None of that occurs to you if you don't have an intuition for where the time is actually going.

And finally, the numbers change. Networks have gotten faster, SSDs have essentially replaced the disk seek number for many workloads, memory bandwidth keeps growing. So people should periodically refresh their mental table. But the habit of thinking in terms of these costs, of doing the estimate before you build, that's the thing I'd most want programmers to take away from it.

r001.rationale: It recommends back-of-the-envelope estimates before coding to assess feasibility and rethink a design, and applies latency comparisons to choices such as sequential versus random access and compression.

r002.rationale: It recommends building a general mental model of operation costs, but does not specifically recommend developing execution-time intuitions for operations in the higher-level libraries a programmer uses.

astra-6.text:
I think of those numbers as a way to build intuition, rather than as constants you should memorize precisely. The useful thing is understanding the relative costs: a reference to memory, reading from a storage device, sending a request to another machine, or sending it across the world. Those are very different operations, and your design should reflect that.

If you’re sketching out a system, you can do a little back-of-the-envelope calculation. How much data do I need to read? How many network round trips are on the critical path? Do those requests have to happen sequentially, or can I issue them in parallel? That can tell you pretty quickly whether a design is even in the right ballpark for your latency target.

It also helps you identify where to spend effort. If you’re waiting on a bunch of sequential remote requests, saving a few instructions locally probably isn’t going to matter much. Batching requests or changing where the data lives might matter a lot.

And then you measure. The particular numbers change with hardware and with the environment you’re running in. The intuition helps you choose a promising design; measurement tells you whether your assumptions were right.

r001.rationale: It recommends back-of-the-envelope estimates to check whether a design meets a latency target, but does not clearly say to use them to compare design alternatives.

r002.rationale: It recommends building intuition about relative costs of memory, storage, and network operations, but does not mention operations in higher-level libraries.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most useful thing is to build an intuition for the relative costs of different operations. You don’t need to memorize every number, and the exact numbers change as hardware evolves. But understanding that accessing main memory is much more expensive than accessing a cache, or that sending a request across a data center is very different from sending one across the world, helps you make better design decisions.

You can use those estimates to do a quick back-of-the-envelope calculation before you build something. How many round trips does this operation require? How much data do we need to read? Can we batch requests or do independent work in parallel? Often that’s enough to tell you whether a design is plausible or whether you need a different approach.

Then you should measure the actual system. The numbers give you a starting point and help you understand what you’re measuring; they don’t replace measurement.

r001.rationale: It recommends back-of-the-envelope calculations before building to assess whether a design is plausible and whether a different approach is needed.

r002.rationale: It discusses intuition about relative costs of memory, cache, and network operations, but does not recommend building intuition for execution times in higher-level libraries.
